nameStory: Woolgrass gets its name from its fluffy, woolly-looking flower clusters that appear in late summer. Each tiny flower has six long, hair-like bristles that stick out from the seed head, creating a soft, cottony appearance that resembles sheep's wool. Despite the name, it's not actually a grass at all — it's a sedge!
description: Woolgrass is a clump-forming wetland sedge that grows 2-4 feet tall in dense colonies. It produces upright stems topped with distinctive fluffy, brownish flower clusters that look like cotton balls or wool tufts. The plant has long, narrow leaves that can reach over 2 feet in length and about half an inch wide. In late summer and fall, the woolly seed heads become the plant's most recognizable feature, often persisting into winter.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Distinctive woolly, cotton-like flower clusters appear in late summer, with long hair-like bristles extending from small reddish-brown to blackish scales, giving the entire seed head a fuzzy, soft appearance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow leaves up to 2+ feet long and about half an inch wide, with 5-10 leaves per stem; lower leaf sheaths may be greenish or reddish

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense clumps or colonies from underground rhizomes, with upright fertile stems reaching 2-4 feet tall in wet areas

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Woolly seed heads persist well into winter, turning from brown to grayish and maintaining their fluffy texture even when dry

habitat: Woolgrass thrives in various wetland habitats including marshes, pond edges, wet meadows, and swampy areas throughout New England. You'll often find it growing alongside cattails, sedges, and other marsh plants in both natural wetlands and disturbed wet areas like roadside ditches. It prefers consistently moist to wet soils and can tolerate both sunny and partially shaded locations.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge from established clumps, with fresh leaves unfurling. Plants focus on vegetative growth during this season.
seasonality.summer: Leaves reach full size and the distinctive woolly flower clusters begin to develop in mid to late summer, starting as compact brownish heads.
seasonality.fall: The woolly seed heads are at their most prominent, fully fluffy and cottony in appearance. This is the best time to identify woolgrass by its characteristic features.
seasonality.winter: Dried woolly seed heads often persist on dead stems, appearing grayish and somewhat flattened but still recognizable. Dead leaves may remain attached to the base.

funFact: Native American tribes found woolgrass so useful that the Potawatomi people stuffed their pillows with its soft, woolly seed heads — essentially creating the world's first natural down alternative! The Ojibwa also wove the tough stems into durable bags and mats.
confusionNotes: Woolgrass might be confused with cattails from a distance, but cattails have the distinctive brown "hot dog" shaped flower spikes, while woolgrass has fluffy, cotton-like clusters. Remember: if it looks like cotton balls, it's woolgrass; if it looks like corn dogs, it's cattails.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "woolgrass," this plant is actually a sedge, not a grass. Sedges belong to a different plant family entirely and can be remembered by the saying "sedges have edges" — their stems are typically triangular rather than round like true grasses. The "bulrush" part of its alternate name is also misleading, as bulrushes are sedges, not true rushes.
compareHints: Woolgrass can be distinguished from other bulrushes in its genus by its particularly fluffy, wool-like seed heads with prominent bristles. Dark green bulrush has similar growth habits but lacks the distinctly woolly appearance, while panicled bulrush tends to be taller with more open, spreading flower clusters. The cottony texture of woolgrass seed heads is more pronounced than in its relatives, making it one of the easier bulrushes to identify when in flower.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its bulrush relatives, panicled bulrush stands out with its distinctly loose, branching flower cluster - woolgrass has a denser, more cotton-like appearance, while nodding bulrush has drooping clusters on curved branches.
**Uncertain comparisons** - Unlike the robust woolgrass or dark green bulrush which form substantial clumps, mosquito bulrush likely maintains a more delicate, scattered growth pattern.
Among New England's bulrushes, dark green bulrush stands out for its robust size and deep green color.

Among its Scirpus relatives, black-girdle bulrush is the only one with the distinctive dark stem bands - woolgrass has woolly flower heads, dark green bulrush lacks the bands and is more robust, and panicled bulrush has much larger, more open flower clusters.
Among its Scirpus relatives in New England, nodding bulrush stands out for its distinctly drooping flower clusters - most other bulrushes like woolgrass have more upright, dense flower heads.
Among its bulrush relatives, Long's bulrush stands out for its coastal habitat preference and rare flowering habit - most other bulrushes in the genus flower more regularly.

**[UNCERTAIN CLAIM]** Unlike its wetland relatives like woolgrass and dark green bulrush which form dense stands in sunny marshes, Woodland Beakrush grows in small, scattered clumps in shaded forests.
Among its bulrush relatives in New England, Georgia bulrush is much less common than woolgrass or dark green bulrush, which you're more likely to encounter in similar wet habitats.

Among New England bulrushes, leafy bulrush stands out for having numerous well-developed leaves along the stem, while woolgrass has a more densely clustered, wool-like flower head, and dark green bulrush tends to be shorter with darker foliage.
Unlike its close relative mosquito bulrush which it sometimes hybridizes with, northeastern bulrush has those distinctive barbed bristles on its fruits.
Among New England's bulrushes, stalked bulrush is the only one with flower clusters that hang from individual stalks rather than sitting directly on the main stem.
